title: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
summary: Map many spellings of one company, school or title to one ID: clean, block, score with Fellegi-Sunter, estimate it by EM, compare learned matchers, cluster, evaluate, and link to registries and O*NET.
outcomes: Build a cleaning step with NFKC, case folding and suffix stripping, and explain what each one removes.
Compute reduction ratio and pairs completeness for blocking rules and sorted neighbourhood.
Compute Fellegi-Sunter weights, estimate m, u and lambda by random sampling and EM, and apply term-frequency adjustments.
Choose between a Fellegi-Sunter model, an actively learned classifier, a fine-tuned transformer and an LLM matcher.
Explain how thresholds, connected components and centroid linkage cause missed or false merges, and keep IDs stable.
Evaluate clusters with pairwise and B-cubed metrics and explain when they disagree.
Link companies and schools to a knowledge base with aliases, hierarchies, renames and ambiguous acronyms.
Map job titles to O*NET-SOC codes with aliases, a seniority parser and embeddings, and know where each fails.

lessons.title: Why raw strings break filters and joins

blocks.md: A recruiter types the filter **company = Quantix**. Three profiles in the index really did work at Quantix, but their members typed the company as `Quantix, Inc.`, `QAUNTIX` and `Ｑｕａｎｔｉｘ Inc` (in full-width letters). An exact string filter matches none of them. The ranking can be perfect and the result is still wrong, because the right candidates never reach it.

**Entity normalization** fixes this by mapping every surface form of a real-world thing (a company, a school, a job title) to one **canonical ID**, and filtering, joining and counting on that ID. The same problem appears under many names: statisticians say **record linkage**, database people say **entity resolution** or **deduplication**, and Peter Christen's survey of indexing techniques for record linkage, a main source for this course, lists more (merge/purge, data matching, reference reconciliation).

Two flavors share the same machinery:

1. **Linking to a reference list.** A catalog of canonical entities already exists (a company registry, a list of schools, the occupation codes of O*NET) and each raw string must be mapped to one entry. That catalog, the Occupational Information Network, is the US Department of Labor's database of occupations; its codes extend the government's Standard Occupational Classification (SOC), so the combined codes are named after both.
2. **Deduplication.** No catalog exists. You must decide which records refer to the same entity and invent an ID per group.

This course walks one toy dataset of 8 company records through the full pipeline: clean, block, compare, score, cluster, then shows how the model's parameters are estimated, how learned matchers compare and how to measure the result. The last two lessons link companies and schools to public registries and job titles to a taxonomy.

blocks.title: The record linkage pipeline

scenes.caption: Raw records arrive with case, punctuation, Unicode and suffix variation. Every later step is cheaper and more accurate if these are standardized first.
Comparing every record with every other is quadratic. Blocking keeps only pairs that share a cheap key, such as the first letters of the cleaned name.
Each candidate pair is compared field by field (name, city, domain). The result is a comparison vector: which fields agree exactly, roughly, or not at all.
A scoring model turns the comparison vector into a match weight. High scores become links, low scores are dropped, and the uncertain middle can go to a human reviewer.
Links are pairwise. Clustering turns them into groups, and each group gets one canonical ID that filters and joins use from then on.

blocks.md: Normalize to an ID, filter on the ID, and keep the raw string for display and debugging. Run the **same** normalizer on queries and on profiles, or the two sides drift apart and matches silently disappear.

blocks.question: A team stores only the canonical company ID and discards the raw string to save space. What goes wrong first?
options: Nothing: the canonical ID carries all the information that was in the raw string
Filters become slower because IDs are longer than names
When the matcher makes a mistake or the taxonomy changes, there is no way to audit or re-run normalization on the original input
Fuzzy matching stops working because IDs cannot be compared with edit distance
blocks.explain: Normalization is a lossy, model-driven step that will be wrong sometimes and will be improved over time. Keeping the raw string lets you show members what they typed, debug bad merges and re-normalize everything when the alias table or model changes.

blocks.question: Which situation is deduplication rather than linking to a reference list?
options: Mapping job titles to O*NET-SOC occupation codes
Grouping company names scraped from resumes when no company registry is available
Mapping school names to a fixed list of accredited universities
blocks.explain: With a reference list, each string is matched to an existing entry. Without one, you must discover the groups themselves and mint IDs for them, which is deduplication. Both use cleaning, blocking and pairwise scoring.

lessons.title: Cleaning: Unicode, case, punctuation and legal suffixes

blocks.md: Cleaning (Christen calls it *cleaning and standardisation*) converts raw input into one consistent form before anything is compared. It is deterministic, cheap and runs on every record and every query. It does not decide whether two records match; it removes differences that are never meaningful so that the later, expensive steps only see real differences.

**Unicode normalization first.** The same visible text can be stored as different code points. Unicode Standard Annex #15 defines four normalization forms. Their names are short codes: NF stands for normalization form, D stands for decomposed (a character split into a base letter plus combining marks), C for composed (recombined into single code points where possible), and K means compatibility mappings are applied too. NFD and NFC handle *canonical* equivalence (for example `é` as one code point versus `e` plus a combining accent). NFKD and NFKC also apply *compatibility* mappings, which remove formatting distinctions: the `ﬁ` ligature becomes `f` and `i`, full-width letters become ASCII letters, and the Roman numeral `Ⅳ` becomes `IV`. For matching keys, NFKC is the usual choice.

**Case folding second.** Python's `str.casefold()` is like `lower()` but more aggressive, because it is meant for caseless matching: the docs' example is German `ß`, which `lower()` leaves alone and `casefold()` turns into `ss`. So `Müller Straße GmbH` and `MÜLLER STRASSE GMBH` only compare equal after casefolding.

blocks.title: Tracing clean_name on two toy records
blocks.code:
import re, unicodedata

LEGAL = {"inc", "llc", "ltd", "corp", "corporation", "co", "gmbh"}

def clean_name(raw):
    s = unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", raw)
    s = s.casefold()
    s = re.sub(r"[^\w\s]", " ", s)
    s = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", s).strip()
    tokens = [t for t in s.split() if t not in LEGAL]
    return " ".join(tokens)

clean_name("Ｑｕａｎｔｉｘ Inc")
clean_name("Brightline Labs, Inc.")

scenes.caption: Record r7 arrives in full-width letters. NFKC maps each full-width letter to its ASCII compatibility equivalent. The string is still 11 characters, but now plain ASCII.
Case folding removes case distinctions. For ASCII it is the same as lowercasing.
Punctuation becomes spaces and runs of whitespace collapse. Nothing to do for r7.
Legal-form tokens are dropped. r7 is now exactly `quantix`, identical to cleaned r5.
Record r3: NFKC changes nothing (it is already ASCII), casefold lowercases it.
The comma and the period become spaces, then whitespace collapses: `brightline labs inc`.
Dropping `inc` gives `brightline labs`, identical to cleaned r1 (`Brightline Labs LLC`) and r2.

blocks.md: After cleaning, our 8 names become: r1, r2, r3 `brightline labs`; r4 `brightline media`; r5, r7 `quantix`; r6 `qauntix`; r8 `quanta health`. Cities get the same treatment plus a small alias table (`Austin, TX` becomes `austin`; a table entry maps `sf` to `san francisco`).

blocks.prompt: Cleaning made r5 and r7 identical. What does it do for r6, `QAUNTIX`?
blocks.reveal: It becomes `qauntix`, which still differs from `quantix` by a transposition. Cleaning only removes differences that are **never** meaningful; it cannot know that `qauntix` is a typo rather than another company. That judgment needs fuzzy comparison and other fields, which is what the scoring lessons add. (With the Jaro-Winkler formula from the prerequisite course, `quantix` and `qauntix` score 0.957.)

blocks.md: **Alias tables** carry the knowledge that rules cannot derive: abbreviations (`sr` to `senior`, `swe` to `software engineer`), known nicknames and former names, and city aliases. They are simple dictionaries applied token by token or to the whole string, and they are often the highest-precision part of the system (precision is the share of the matches it makes that are correct) because a human wrote each entry.

Stripping is lossy. NFKC turns the superscript in `i⁹` into a plain `9`, and a stopword list (words deleted from every key because they seem uninformative) that drops `group`, `bank` or `the` can merge different companies. Strip only tokens that never distinguish entities in your data, apply cleaning to the matching key, and keep the original string.
Version the normalizer. If a new suffix rule changes the key for 2% of records, every index built with the old key must be rebuilt, or queries and profiles stop matching.

blocks.question: Which single step makes `Ｑｕａｎｔｉｘ` (full-width) equal to `Quantix`?
options: Case folding with casefold()
Unicode NFC normalization
Unicode NFKC normalization
Removing punctuation
blocks.explain: Full-width letters are compatibility characters. Only the K forms (NFKD, NFKC) apply compatibility mappings; NFC handles canonical equivalence only and leaves them unchanged. Case folding does not map full-width letters to ASCII.

blocks.question: Profiles are cleaned with NFKC, casefold and suffix stripping before indexing. The query parser lowercases the recruiter's text but does nothing else. A recruiter searches `Brightline Labs, Inc.`. What happens?
options: It matches, because lowercasing is enough
It misses: the query key is `brightline labs, inc.` while the indexed key is `brightline labs`
It matches only r3, which was typed the same way
blocks.explain: The index stores cleaned keys, so a raw query string with a comma and suffix never equals them. The fix is to run the exact same normalizer on the query side.

lessons.title: Blocking: compare only pairs that could match

blocks.md: Deduplicating $n$ records means up to $n(n-1)/2$ pairs: each of the $n$ records can pair with $n-1$ others, and that counts every pair twice (A with B and B with A), so we halve it. Two open-source Python libraries are references throughout: dedupe (from DataMade) and Splink (from the UK Ministry of Justice). The dedupe docs work the numbers: 1,000 records give 499,500 pairs, and 100,000 records give 4,999,950,000. Splink's docs note that 1 million records produce about 500 billion comparisons (our script: 499,999,500,000). Detailed field comparison is the bottleneck, so comparing every pair is out of the question beyond small data.

**Blocking** (Christen's survey calls the general step *indexing*) puts records into blocks by a cheap **blocking key** and compares only pairs inside a block. Christen points out the core asymmetry: comparisons grow quadratically with data size while true matches grow only linearly, so the vast majority of all pairs are non-matches that should never be compared. To estimate the saving, split $n$ records into $b$ equal blocks: each block holds $n/b$ records and so has $(n/b)(n/b-1)/2$ pairs, and multiplying by the $b$ blocks gives $(n/2)(n/b-1)$.

blocks.caption: Christen's estimate for deduplication with b uniformly sized blocks. With n = 1,000,000 and b = 10,000 blocks: 49,500,000 pairs instead of about 500 billion. Real key values are skewed (many 'Smith'), so the largest blocks dominate.

blocks.title: Candidate pairs with and without blocking

scenes.caption: Without blocking, pairs grow with n squared: 1 million records give about 5 x 10^11 pairs.
With 1,000 equal blocks, 1 million records need about 5 x 10^8 pairs, a 1,000x cut (simplified: assumes uniform block sizes).
More, smaller blocks cut work further, but each extra split raises the chance that two true duplicates land in different blocks and are never compared.

blocks.md:
On our 8 records ($28$ possible pairs) we use two blocking rules on the *cleaned* fields, and keep a pair if **either** rule fires, as Splink does with a list of rules:

- **B1:** same first 3 characters of the cleaned name.
- **B2:** same website domain (missing domains never match).

blocks.title: Two blocking rules on the toy records

scenes.caption: 8 cleaned records, 28 possible pairs. Before cleaning, the prefixes would be `Bri`, `bri`, `Qua`, `QAU` and full-width `Ｑｕａ`, splitting true duplicates: clean before you block.
B1 (name prefix) makes blocks `bri` = {r1, r2, r3, r4}, `qua` = {r5, r7, r8} and `qau` = {r6}: 6 + 3 = 9 pairs. The typo puts r6 in a block by itself.
B2 (same domain) gives pairs r1-r2 and r5-r6. The second one is new: the domain rescues the typo record r6.

The union has 10 candidate pairs instead of 28: reduction ratio (the share of pairs skipped) 1 - 10/28 = 0.643. Five of the 10 are true matches (pairs quality, the share of candidates that are true, 0.5).
One true pair, r6-r7, shares no key: r6 has the typo and r7 has no domain. Pairs completeness (the share of true pairs kept) is 5/6 = 0.833. Lesson 7 shows clustering can still recover it through r5.

blocks.md:
Christen defines three measures for the blocking step, with $s_M$ and $s_N$ the true matches and non-matches among candidate pairs, and $n_M$, $n_N$ the totals among all possible pairs:

- **Reduction ratio** $RR = 1 - (s_M + s_N)/(n_M + n_N)$: how much work was cut. Toy: 0.643.
- **Pairs completeness** $PC = s_M / n_M$: recall of true pairs. Toy: 5/6 = 0.833.
- **Pairs quality** $PQ = s_M/(s_M + s_N)$: precision of candidates. Toy: 5/10 = 0.5.

A pair that blocking drops is classified as a non-match without ever being looked at. No scoring model can recover it. Use several strict rules joined by OR (Splink's advice: a longer list of strict rules beats a short list of loose ones), so a typo in one field is caught by a rule on another.

Libraries automate this. The dedupe library offers **predicates**, rules that compute blocking keys from a field, such as *first 3 characters*, *token field* (records sharing any whole word) and *common 4-gram* (records sharing any run of 4 consecutive characters). It learns which combination to use with Chvatal's greedy set-cover algorithm. Set cover means choosing a small set of rules whose blocks together contain every labeled duplicate pair; greedy means adding rules one at a time, each time the one that covers the most still-uncovered pairs for its cost, here the comparisons it adds.

Christen's survey compares six indexing families: traditional blocking (exact key values, as above); sorted neighbourhood (sort records by a key and compare only records inside a small sliding window); q-gram indexing (keys built from sub-lists of a key's q-grams, its runs of q characters, so keys that differ by a typo can still share a block); canopy clustering (a cheap similarity puts records into overlapping groups); string-map (strings become points in a space that keeps their distances, and nearby points are grouped); and suffix-array indexing (records whose keys share a long enough suffix land together).

**Sorted neighbourhood on the toy.** Sort the records by a key (here the cleaned name, ties broken by record id) and slide a window of $w$ records down the sorted list, comparing every pair inside the window. Records whose keys differ only near the end of the string still sort next to each other, which is exactly what a prefix block cannot do for `qauntix`: in sort order it falls between `brightline media` and `quanta health`, two places away from the first `quantix`.

blocks.title: Sorted neighbourhood, window 3, on the 8 cleaned names

scenes.caption: The 8 records sorted by cleaned name (only the first 6 letters fit in a cell). `qauntix` sorts before `quanta health` because a comes before u in the second letter.
The window covers positions 0 to 2: pairs r1-r2, r1-r3, r2-r3, all true matches. Then it slides down one position at a time.
Window at positions 4 to 6 holds r6, r8 and r5. The typo record r6 now meets r5 by name alone, with no help from the domain rule.
Last window, positions 5 to 7: r8, r5, r7 gives the true pair r5-r7. r6 and r7 are 3 places apart, so r6-r7 is never compared. Totals: 13 pairs, RR 0.536, PC 5/6 = 0.833, PQ 0.385.
Break every tie the other way (descending record id, so r7 before r5) and r6 meets r7 instead of r5: same counts, different pair. With window 4 all 6 true pairs are found, at 18 pairs (RR 0.357).

blocks.md:
Our script's numbers for the toy, side by side (RR reduction ratio, PC pairs completeness, PQ pairs quality):

- B1 name prefix alone: 9 pairs, RR 0.679, PC 4/6 = 0.667, PQ 0.444.
- B2 same domain alone: 2 pairs, RR 0.929, PC 2/6 = 0.333, PQ 1.0.
- B1 or B2: 10 pairs, RR 0.643, PC 5/6 = 0.833, PQ 0.5.
- Sorted neighbourhood, window 3: 13 pairs, RR 0.536, PC 5/6 = 0.833, PQ 0.385.

Sorted neighbourhood reaches the same completeness as the two-rule union using one field only, at the cost of 3 more pairs. Which true pair it finds depends on window size and tie order, so production systems run several passes with different sort keys.

blocks.question: You block company records on the first 3 letters of the raw (uncleaned) name. Which true duplicate pair is most likely to be lost?
options: `Quantix, Inc.` and `Ｑｕａｎｔｉｘ Inc`
`Quantix, Inc.` and `Quantix Inc`
`Brightline Labs LLC` and `Brightline Labs, Inc.`
blocks.explain: Full-width letters are different code points, so the raw prefixes differ even though the text looks identical. The other two pairs share the raw prefix `Qua` or `Bri`. Blocking keys must be computed from cleaned values.

blocks.question: Adding a third rule, *same city*, to our toy blocking would do what?
options: Raise pairs completeness to 1.0 and keep the candidate count at 10
Recover r6-r7 (both Denver) but add many more pairs, lowering the reduction ratio
Have no effect, because city is not a name field
blocks.explain: City is low-cardinality (it has few distinct values): everyone in Austin would be paired with everyone else in Austin. It recovers r6-r7 but at a large cost in comparisons on real data. A stricter combined key (city plus name prefix of 2 letters, say) is the usual compromise.

lessons.title: Scoring pairs with Fellegi-Sunter match weights

blocks.md: For each candidate pair we compare fields and record a **comparison vector** $\gamma$: for example name *exact*, city *exact*, domain *missing*. Splink calls each field's test a *comparison* with ordered **comparison levels**, checked like an if/elif chain (its docs example: exact match, Jaro-Winkler above 0.95, above 0.8, everything else). We use three: name (exact, Jaro-Winkler at least 0.88, else), city (exact, else) and domain (exact, else, or no evidence if missing).

Fellegi and Sunter (1969) framed linkage as hypothesis testing: for every pair, decide between two hypotheses, the records match or they do not, from the evidence in its comparison vector. Each level has two probabilities:

- $m$ is the probability of seeing this level when the records truly match. It measures data quality: true duplicates agree on city most of the time, but typos and moves happen.
- $u$ is the probability of seeing this level when the records do not match. It measures coincidence: two unrelated companies share a city far more often than a website domain.

blocks.caption: Splink's form, in words: each field adds its weight w, log2 of m over u; the total M is the prior's weight plus every field's weight; P(match) is 2 to the M over 1 plus 2 to the M. The prior lambda is the probability that two random records match.

blocks.md: Where the formula comes from: Bayes' rule written with **odds**, $P/(1-P)$. Before looking at any field, the odds of a match are $\lambda/(1-\lambda)$. Seeing a level multiplies those odds by $m/u$, how much more likely that level is among matches than among non-matches: an exact city match has $0.90/0.05 = 18$, so it makes a match 18 times likelier. If fields are independent given match status, the multipliers of all fields simply multiply. Taking $\log_2$ turns that product into a sum, so each field adds $w = \log_2(m/u)$ (for city, $\log_2 18 = 4.17$) and every +1 of weight doubles the odds. Converting the final odds, 2 to the power M, back into a probability gives 2 to the M over 1 plus 2 to the M, the formula above.

Assumed parameters for the toy (illustrative values of the kind Splink estimates; the next lesson shows how: $u$ from random record pairs, which are almost all non-matches, and $m$ by expectation maximisation, worked by hand on these 10 pairs):

- name: exact $m$=0.70, $u$=0.002 (w = 8.45); fuzzy 0.25, 0.01 (w = 4.64); else 0.05, 0.988 (w = -4.30)
- city: exact 0.90, 0.05 (w = 4.17); else 0.10, 0.95 (w = -3.25)
- domain: exact 0.85, 0.001 (w = 9.73); else 0.15, 0.999 (w = -2.74); missing: w = 0
- prior $\lambda$ = 0.001, so the prior weight is $\log_2(0.001/0.999) = -9.96$

blocks.prompt: r1 and r3 have the same cleaned name and city, but r3 has no domain. Using the weights above, is the match probability above or below 0.95?
blocks.reveal: **Below: 0.863.** The weight is -9.96 + 8.45 + 4.17 + 0 = 2.66, and $2^{2.66}/(1+2^{2.66}) = 0.863$. Agreement on name and city is strong evidence, but it must overcome a prior of 1 in 1,000. Without the domain there is not enough evidence to be 95% sure.

blocks.title: Match weight, one field at a time

scenes.caption: r1-r2: every field agrees exactly. Total 12.39, probability 0.9998. (Bars show size; the number shows the sign.)
r1-r3: same name and city, domain missing, so it adds 0. Total 2.66, probability 0.863: likely but not certain.
r5-r6: the typo drops name to the fuzzy level (4.64 instead of 8.45), but the shared domain adds 9.73. Total 8.58, probability 0.997.
r1-r4 (labs vs media, Jaro-Winkler 0.91): fuzzy name plus same city, no domain. Total -1.15, probability 0.311. Different companies, but the evidence is thin.
r5-r8: name, city and domain all disagree. Total -20.25, probability about 0.0000008.

blocks.title: Weights for all 10 candidate pairs

scenes.caption: Per-field weights for each candidate pair (total includes the -9.96 prior). Red-blue scale: positive is evidence for a match.
Seven pairs have a missing domain, so that column contributes 0 and they lean entirely on name and city.
Totals: r1-r2 (12.39) and r5-r6 (8.58) are clear links; r5-r8 and r7-r8 are clear non-links; the 2.66 and -1.15 rows are the uncertain middle.

blocks.md: Fellegi and Sunter's decision rule has **three** outcomes, not two: *link*, *non-link* and *possible link*. Sort pairs by weight, choose an upper threshold for an acceptable false-link rate and a lower threshold for an acceptable missed-link rate, and send everything in between to clerical review, where a person checks them. Their theorem shows this rule minimizes the number of possible links (human work) for the chosen error levels.

blocks.title: From summed evidence to match probability

scenes.caption: With prior -9.96, the evidence must sum to 14.2 to reach P = 0.95. Only r1-r2 and r5-r6 clear the accept line.
r1-r3, r2-r3, r5-r7 (0.863) and r1-r4, r2-r4, r3-r4 (0.311) sit between the lines: 6 of 10 pairs go to review, mostly because the domain is missing.

Raise the prior to -6.63 (lambda = 0.01) and the curve shifts left. The plotted points do not move with the slider: they were computed at lambda = 0.001. The prior encodes how rare matches are in the data.

blocks.md: The independence assumption double-counts correlated fields. Company name and website domain usually agree or disagree together, so adding both full weights overstates the evidence. Merge strongly correlated fields into one comparison, or check calibration on labeled pairs: whether pairs scored 0.9 really match about 90% of the time.
Each field adds $\log_2(m/u)$. Agreement on a rare value (a domain) is worth far more than agreement on a common one (a city), and a missing field adds nothing instead of counting as a disagreement.

blocks.question: City has m = 0.90 and u = 0.05 for exact agreement. A new data source has many members who typed their home city instead of the company's HQ city, so true duplicates agree on city only 45% of the time. What happens to the exact-city weight?
options: It stays 4.17 because u did not change
It drops to log2(0.45/0.05) = 3.17
It becomes negative
It doubles, because more disagreement means more information
blocks.explain: m measures how often true matches agree. Halving m from 0.90 to 0.45 subtracts exactly 1 from log2(m/u). Disagreement also becomes less damning: the else weight rises from log2(0.10/0.95) = -3.25 to log2(0.55/0.95) = -0.79.

blocks.question: Why is a missing domain scored as weight 0 rather than with the disagree weight -2.74?
options: Missing data carries no evidence either way; scoring it as disagreement would push true duplicates like r1-r3 toward non-match
Because log2 of zero is undefined
Because Fellegi-Sunter only allows agreement levels
blocks.explain: A missing value is neither agreement nor disagreement. Treating it as disagreement subtracts 2.74 and would drop r1-r3 from 0.863 to about 0.49, punishing incomplete records rather than conflicting ones.

lessons.title: Estimating m and u: random sampling, EM and term frequencies

blocks.md: The scoring lesson assumed every $m$ and $u$. Real data has no labels, so they must be estimated from the records themselves. Splink's training guide recommends three steps in this order: estimate the prior $\lambda$ directly, estimate $u$ from random record pairs, then estimate $m$ by expectation maximisation (EM). Its stated reason is empirical: direct estimates of $\lambda$ and $u$ gave better parameters and fewer convergence problems than learning everything with EM.

**$\lambda$ first.** You write a few strict deterministic rules you believe only true matches satisfy (same first name, surname and date of birth, say) plus a guess of their recall, the share of all matches they catch. Splink counts the rule hits and scales by the recall. The guess can be rough: if the true recall is 80% and the true prior weight is -14, guessing 60% or 95% scales $\lambda$ by 0.8/0.6 or 0.8/0.95, so the weight moves only to about -13.58 or -14.25 (the docs' own example quotes -13.75 and -14.42).

**$u$ from random pairs.** Two records drawn at random are almost never the same entity, so the share of random pairs that agree on a field estimates $u$, the agreement rate among non-matches. We test this on FEBRL1, a public synthetic dataset from Christen's Febrl record-linkage package, shipped with the Python `recordlinkage` library (the code below runs Splink on DuckDB, an in-process SQL database engine): 1,000 person records, 500 originals plus exactly one corrupted duplicate each. That is 499,500 pairs, of which 500 match, so the true $\lambda$ is 0.001.

blocks.code:
import recordlinkage.datasets as rds
import splink.comparison_library as cl
from splink import DuckDBAPI, Linker, SettingsCreator, block_on

df, true_links = rds.load_febrl1(return_links=True)
df = df.reset_index().rename(columns={"rec_id": "unique_id"})
settings = SettingsCreator(link_type="dedupe_only", comparisons=[
    cl.JaroWinklerAtThresholds("given_name", [0.9]),
    cl.JaroWinklerAtThresholds("surname", [0.9]),
    cl.ExactMatch("date_of_birth"), cl.ExactMatch("suburb"),
    cl.ExactMatch("postcode")],
  blocking_rules_to_generate_predictions=[block_on("surname"),
